lesson.title: The Currency of Light: How Photons Carry Energy
lesson.summary: Light delivers energy in discrete packets called photons, and the energy of each photon depends only on its frequency. This idea launched quantum theory and gives chemists a precise tool for probing atoms and molecules.
lesson.body:
Light is often described as a wave with a frequency and a wavelength, but by the early twentieth century physicists realized that light also behaves as a stream of discrete energy packets called photons. Each photon carries a fixed, non-divisible amount of energy that depends only on the frequency of the light, not on how bright or dim the beam is. This builds directly on two ideas you already have in hand: frequency, the number of wave cycles passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz, or cycles per second), and energy, the capacity to do work or transfer heat, measured in joules (J). Photon energy is simply the bridge that connects those two quantities for a beam of light.

The relationship is remarkably simple: E = hf, where E is the energy of a single photon, f is the frequency of the light, and h is Planck's constant, a fixed conversion factor equal to 6.626 x 10^-34 joule seconds. Because h is constant, energy and frequency rise and fall together: double the frequency and you double the energy per photon. This is why the electromagnetic spectrum forms an energy ladder. Radio waves, with frequencies around 10^6 Hz, carry almost no energy per photon. Visible light sits in the middle. Ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma ray photons, with frequencies of 10^16 Hz and higher, carry enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms or break chemical bonds entirely.

Consider a beam of green light with a wavelength of 550 nanometers (550 x 10^-9 m), close to what the human eye perceives as the brightest part of the visible spectrum. Its frequency is f = c / lambda = (3.00 x 10^8 m/s) / (550 x 10^-9 m) = 5.45 x 10^14 Hz. Multiplying by Planck's constant gives the energy of one photon: E = hf = (6.626 x 10^-34 J s)(5.45 x 10^14 Hz) = 3.61 x 10^-19 J. That is an almost incomprehensibly small number, which makes sense since a single photon is an almost incomprehensibly small object. Converting to electron volts (1 eV = 1.602 x 10^-19 J) gives about 2.25 eV, a convenient unit chemists use for energies at the atomic scale.

Why does this matter for chemistry rather than just physics? Because the energy of a photon determines what it can and cannot do to matter. A photon of visible light carries just enough energy to nudge a valence electron into a higher orbital, which is why colored compounds absorb specific wavelengths. A photon of ultraviolet light carries enough energy to break some chemical bonds outright, which is why UV exposure damages DNA and degrades plastics. A single photon of infrared light, by contrast, is usually too weak to do either and instead just makes molecules vibrate and rotate a little faster, which we feel as heat. Chemists exploit this energy ladder constantly, choosing a light source with exactly the photon energy needed for a given job.

This quantization of light energy was a genuinely radical idea when Max Planck introduced it in 1900 and Albert Einstein extended it in 1905. Classical physics predicted that light energy should be continuous and adjustable to any value simply by changing the brightness of the source. Photon energy shows instead that energy arrives in fixed, countable packets, with only the number of photons, not their individual energy, changing when you turn up the brightness. That single shift in thinking opens the door to everything that follows: Planck's equation, the photoelectric effect, and the discrete line spectra that reveal how electrons are arranged inside atoms.
